Note: the following text is a mixture of what I said, what I think I said, and what I wish I said.
As such, there may be small discrepancies from the lecture.
Of course, there may be errors, and there is no peer-review.

This semester, we are preparing a submission for CG:SHOP [@cgshop], part of the annual Symposium on Computational Geometry (SoCG).
The problem for this year is *multi-robot lawn mowing*:

- **input**: axis-aligned polygonal regions $R$ (lawn) and $\chi$ (cutter), and a parameter $k$
- **output**: axis-aligned tours $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k$ such that $\bigcup_{i \in \arange{k}} \bigcup_{p_j \in \tau_i} \chi(p_j) \supseteq R$, minimizing $\max_{i \in \arange{k}} \abs{\tau_i}$

Here, I am using the notation $\arange{k} = \set{1, \ldots, k}$, $\chi(p)$ to denote placing the cutter centered at point $p$.
All regions are in the plane $\R^2$.
For this problem in particular, each edge of a region has integer side lengths, and so do the output tours (I will refer to this as integrality).
See the 2nd meeting ([www.cstheory.org/meetings/](https://www.cstheory.org/meetings/)) for a slides/video description.

Now, this is a difficult problem to try and reason about.
For example, some of the challenges include:

- an infinite amount of potential tours and different regions;
  moreover without integrality, it is uncountable!
- arbitrary regions $R$ and $\chi$ that can be non-convex or be any other nasty shapes
- combinatorial explosion from planning $k$ simultaneous tours

Therefore, for the first few weeks, we shall focus on some special cases which are a bit easier to think about.
For example, we could:

- only consider one robot at a time (avoiding the combinatorial explosion)
- or restrict the shape of the cutter $\chi$ or the region

or there are many other simplifications, as we will later see.
For today (and next week), we will restrict $\chi$ to be a unit square and consider only $k=1$ (one robot).

See [full notes](/files/notes/fa26-cgshop/10-22/notes.pdf).
